This film makes an earnest attempt to discuss fallout and makes several important points about how dangerous it can be. At this time public sentiment was building against nuclear tests. Just two years after this film was released, three (UK, US, Soviet Union) of the four nuclear states and many non-nuclear states signed the 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty, pledging to refrain from testing nuclear weapons in the atmosphere, underwater, or in outer space. Underground testing continued for decades however. The film provides an overview of nuclear radiation, emphasizing the importance of understanding atmospheric contamination from bomb tests and the dangers of nuclear radiations. It explains how radioactive particles from nuclear tests enter the atmosphere and affect food and drink, alongside background radiation from natural sources. It covers exposure to internal and external radiation, the relative safety of man-made radiations from medical X-rays, and the cumulative effects of radiation. DayisNew1942.sy: This poetic and meditative film captures a day in the life of Mexico City, unfolding from the early morning through nightfall. The narration opens as dawn breaks over the valley, likening the waking city to a young girl being gently washed and prepared for the day. Streets come to life as shops lift their shutters and churches open their doors, offering solace to both the devout and the troubled. Children march off to school, markets fill with the vibrant hum of vendors and shoppers, and the gears of daily life grind forward with energy and rhythm. The narrator reflects on Mexico’s rich contrasts—an old land that is constantly renewing, a poor country rich in culture and pride, and a place of both ancient heritage and modern ambition. As factory workers pause for lunch, and newspapers announce the day's headlines, the city also makes space for reflection and pleasure—afternoon walks in Alameda Park, tea and music in Chapultepec. By evening, the shops close, workers return home, and the Zócalo pulses gently with quiet. As bells ring out and the last light fades, the narrator offers a benediction: “All’s well in Mexico this night. All’s well.”

SVS-3349.sy: The Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) satellite was launched on November 27, 1997, as a joint mission of NASA and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, JAXA. TRMM has five Earth-observing instruments on board and circles the Earth every 92 minutes in an equatorial orbit between 35 degrees north and south latitude so that those instruments can measure precipitation in the tropics. One of the instruments, TMI, observes five frequencies of microwave emissions in a 780-kilometer wide swath along the orbit in order to measure the amount of rain and ice in the atmosphere. This animation shows the TRMM satellite orbiting for one day, August 27, 2005, showing a set of TRMM measurements at a frequency of 85.5 GHz. In this frequency band, atmospheric ice crystals scatter microwaves and so areas with ice crystals appear colder than areas with no ice. Both Hurricane Katrina, just to the west of Florida in the Gulf of Mexico, and Typhoon Talim, in the westerm Pacific between Japan and New Guinea, show up as bright swirling patterns. This measurement is just one of the TMI measurements that go into calculating the total instantaneous rainfall in the tropics. Note: This animation shows the TRMM satellite orbiting the Earth on August 27, 2005 by revealing TMI 85.5 GHz microwave measurements for that day. This animation is on a cartesian map projection, so the satellite will look accurate only when the animation is wrapped to a sphere. Data Collected: 2005/08/27T00:45Z -…

bill_trm_200307.sy: After coming ashore on June 30, 2003, just east of Morgan City, Louisiana, the remnants of Tropical Storm Bill continued to produce heavy rain through the southeastern United States and mid-Atlantic region as the system tracked northeastward across the country. The heaviest rainfall totals were along the Gulf Coast east of where Bill made landfall. Some areas between western Louisiana and the Florida panhandle received upwards of 10 inches of rain according to observations from the Multi-satellite Precipitation Analysis, based on data from the trmm.gsfc.nasa.gov/ Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM). The low-pressure center associated with Bill tracked northeastward across western Louisiana, southern Mississippi, and central Alabama before merging with a stationary front over the western Carolinas. Broad areas of 2-4 inch rainfall amounts were observed from northern Alabama and central Georgia through the Carolinas and into northern Virginia with locally heavier amounts of 4-8 inches. Fortunately, the remnants of Tropical Storm Bill moved steadily across the southeast. This kept rainfall amounts from being even higher. TRMM is a joint mission between NASA and the Japanese space agency NASDA.

mopitt_first_year.sy: NASA's terra.nasa.gov Terra spacecraft has assembled the most complete view ever of the world's air pollution traveling through the atmosphere, across continents and oceans. For the first time, policymakers and scientists now have a way to identify the major sources of air pollution and to closely track where the pollution goes, anywhere on Earth. The false colors in these images represent levels of carbon monoxide in the lower atmosphere, ranging from about 390 parts per billion (dark brown pixels), to 220 parts per billion (red pixels), to 50 parts per billion (blue pixels). Carbon monoxide is a gaseous byproduct from the burning of fossil fuels, in industry and automobiles, as well as burning of forests and grasslands. Notice in the April 30, 2000, image that levels of carbon monoxide are much higher in the Northern Hemisphere, where human population and human industry is much greater than in the Southern Hemisphere. However, in the October 30, 2000, image notice the immense plumes of the gas emitted from forest and grassland fires burning in South America and Southern Africa. The movements of carbon monoxide around the globe are particularly striking when viewed as a earthobservatory.nasa.gov/Newsroom/NewImages/Images/mopitt_first_yeara.mpg movie spanning a 10-month period. The new global air pollution monitor onboard Terra is the innovative Measurements Of Pollution In The Troposphere, or MOPITT sensor, which was contributed to the Terra mission by the Canadian Space…

If you hold rights to any material in this archive and wish to discuss its removal, please contact Uncommon Ephemera directly before filing a takedown request with any platform. A takedown removes material immediately and without discussion, and may count as a strike against the Uncommon Ephemera account. Platforms respond to accumulated strikes by removing the account entirely, which would result in the permanent loss of thousands of pieces of historically significant preserved media that have nothing to do with the material in dispute. This is a sound filmstrip that has been fully restored into the included video which properly simulates how it would have been presented originally. PART OF A SET. This filmstrip is part of the set Adventuring With Tiddle The Fiddle. ORIGINAL SCANS AND AUDIO INGEST INCLUDED. The original frame scans and audio capture are included in this archive. whywefightpreludetowarpart1.sy: Why We Fight: Prelude To War Part 1 Reviews events from 1933 to 1939 including the Japanese conquest of Manchuria, the Italian conquest of Ethiopia, the rise of Hitler; and explains the Axis plan of the world conquest. Search Educational Film Journals at Media History Project for references to this film Summary Describes the events leading up to World War II. Shows the development of Fascism in Germany and Italy and the Japanese invasion of Manchuria. Focuses on the rise of the Nazi presence in Germany.
